ai.definition: Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) is a technology that harnesses the natural temperature gradient between warm surface waters and colder deep ocean waters to generate electricity.
ai.howItWorks: OTEC systems typically consist of heat exchangers and turbines. Warm surface water is used to boil a working fluid, which then drives a turbine connected to a generator. Cold deep water is used to condense the vapor back into a liquid, completing the cycle. This process can be used in either open or closed loop configurations.
ai.problemSolved: OTEC addresses the need for sustainable and consistent renewable energy sources that do not rely on variable conditions like wind or solar.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing OTEC plants involves constructing large-scale marine infrastructure, including heat exchangers, turbines, and power generation equipment. The materials used are generally similar to those found in conventional power plant construction, such as steel, concrete, and various alloys.
ai.buildProcess: The build process for an OTEC plant includes site selection, environmental impact assessments, design and engineering, fabrication of components, transportation to the site, installation, testing, and commissioning. The complexity and scale of these projects can vary significantly based on the specific technology used and location.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include high initial capital investment for infrastructure, ongoing maintenance costs, and the cost of deep-water intake systems. Research and development costs are also significant due to the specialized nature of OTEC technology.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: OTEC is expected to grow as more projects come online and technological advancements reduce costs and improve efficiency. However, it remains a niche technology with limited deployment compared to other renewable energy sources.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for OTEC are still developing in many regions. Environmental regulations related to marine ecosystems and water use will likely play a significant role in the adoption of this technology.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include potential impacts on local marine life, thermal pollution from warm water discharge, and structural integrity issues due to corrosion or biofouling. Economic risks stem from high initial costs and uncertain long-term profitability.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently low but expected to improve as technology matures and economies of scale are achieved. However, the limited number of projects means that financial returns remain unpredictable.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development in OTEC could see improvements in efficiency, reduced costs through modular designs, and increased focus on hybrid systems combining OTEC with other renewable technologies or desalination processes.

glossary.def: A substance used in an OTEC system to absorb heat from warm surface water and expand, driving a turbine.
The mechanism for bringing cold deep ocean water to the surface of an OTEC plant to condense vaporized working fluid.
An environmental issue caused by releasing warm water back into the ocean, potentially affecting local marine ecosystems.

subsystems.name: Cold-water pipe
subsystems.role: draws near-freezing seawater from 600–1000 m, the single hardest engineering problem.

subsystems.name: Warm-water intake
subsystems.role: supplies the sun-heated surface layer used as the heat source.

subsystems.name: Heat exchangers
subsystems.role: transfer heat between seawater and the working fluid.

subsystems.name: Power cycle
subsystems.role: a closed Rankine cycle using a fluid that boils at low temperature.

subsystems.name: Platform
subsystems.role: holds the machinery either on land, on a shelf, or afloat.

subsystems.name: Co-product plant
subsystems.role: sells the deep cold water's other benefits to improve the economics.

buildSteps.title: Find a suitable site
buildSteps.detail: You need a sustained temperature difference of roughly 20 °C between surface and deep water, with cold water reachable near shore — mostly tropical coasts and islands.

buildSteps.title: Design the cold-water pipe
buildSteps.detail: Pipe diameter scales with output — roughly a metre across per megawatt — so even small plants need a long, large, cold, moving structure that can survive waves and currents.

buildSteps.title: Build the platform
buildSteps.detail: Either a coastal plant with a trench to the seabed, or a floating hull or barge moored over deep water.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate heat exchangers
buildSteps.detail: Seawater is corrosive, so evaporator and condenser tubes are made from titanium or similar alloys; this is often the largest cost item.

buildSteps.title: Install the cold-water pipe
buildSteps.detail: The pipe is floated out, sunk under control, and its intake lowered to depth — deploying and clamping it is the manoeuvre that most often fails in practice.

buildSteps.title: Fill and commission the cycle
buildSteps.detail: Warm and cold seawater loops are started, the low-boiling-point working fluid is charged, and the turbine is brought up slowly to check parasitic pumping losses.

buildSteps.title: Connect to the grid
buildSteps.detail: A subsea cable carries power ashore; for floating plants it must survive the same motion as the platform.

buildSteps.title: Operate with co-products
buildSteps.detail: Deep water leaving the condenser is cold and nutrient-rich, so desalination, shellfish or fish farming, and seawater air-conditioning are coupled in to make the whole site pay.

prerequisites.why: the pipe and floating platform borrow heavily from offshore oil and gas experience.
seawater destroys ordinary metals, and the heat exchangers dominate capital cost.

prerequisites.tech: Low-boiling-point working fluids and efficient turbines
prerequisites.why: without a fluid that boils on a 20 °C difference there is no cycle.
demonstrated at pilot scale, but no one has built and kept one operating at tens of megawatts.
power must reach shore without erasing the plant's thin margin.
output is small relative to a very large structure, so capital cost per megawatt stays high.

pathway.milestone: pilot plants of roughly 100 kW, mainly on tropical coasts and islands, plus commercial seawater air-conditioning and deep-water aquaculture
pathway.unlocks: operating experience with pipes, heat exchangers and cold-water use.

pathway.milestone: multi-megawatt demonstration plants coupled to desalination and aquaculture
pathway.unlocks: evidence that the co-products can carry the economics.

pathway.milestone: 10–100 MW plants on islands and tropical coasts where diesel generation is expensive
pathway.unlocks: a real niche market, since OTEC runs day and night regardless of weather.

pathway.milestone: large floating plantships with multi-metre cold-water pipes, possibly making hydrogen or ammonia at sea
pathway.unlocks: baseload power and fuel for regions with no shallow-water option.
